name: Zoe Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach beginner recorder at the arts centre two days a week, accompany a small church choir on Saturdays, and copy simple music parts for families. I finished secondary school and still have plenty to learn about teaching; I prefer to watch a skilled player work before I try a new method.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household depending on now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sam works at the bus depot and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The pay is ordinary for this job, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are a few similar posts nearby.

I'd accept a **faster register** without changing my choir or teaching work.
think: I don't use **AI tools**, and small changes leave my paid days in place.
Our **four-month reserve** covers a short gap, though the mortgage keeps me watchful.
do: Ask the **centre** for next term's two teaching days in writing this week.
Keep the **Saturday choir** job and confirmed centre classes.
Save **forty per concert** for the mortgage after family bills clear.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about term renewals but able to cover a short gap.
S0.quote: I won't book a family holiday against a hoped-for teaching term.
fieldNote: Her **four-month reserve** and Sam's depot wage buffer a small booking change.
She watches **term renewals** and avoids AI tools, even when administrative changes are minor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other centre players that a faster register is fine, but the children still need someone to count them in. The Saturday choir has never stayed together because of a neat form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI tools, and a small change would not alter my two teaching days or Saturday church job. We have about four months of expenses saved, though the mortgage means I still check next term's bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the centre for next term's two teaching days in writing this week and keep my Saturday choir slot. After each paid concert this year, I'll put forty into the mortgage reserve if the family bills have cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the term calendar, but I can see four months of bills covered. The choir and my partner's bus depot wages give us some steadiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when one pupil left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One child left the recorder class last spring, and the centre kept the class open. If half the class left, I would ask the manager before assuming the centre would pay me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you plan family spending around a term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the written timetable home to Sam before planning the summer. Our two children ask about holidays, and I have to tell them we're waiting for the timetable. I won't book a family holiday against a hoped-for teaching term.

say: I'd bring **paid-hour records** to the musicians association.
I'd ask the centre to explain **recording consent** before changing pupil practice work.
think: **Registration and practice checks** could cost me one of two teaching days.
Our **four-month reserve** helps, but a long vacancy search would hurt the mortgage.
do: Compare **tutor hours** and bring the figures to the association this month.
Apply for a **library attendant vacancy** after a lost teaching day only if pay and hours fit.
Keep the **Saturday choir** job while seeking replacement work.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible teaching-day cut and mortgage pressure.
S1.quote: A computer can mark practice notes, but the mortgage still wants a person to pay it.
fieldNote: She expects **thinking tasks** to threaten a whole junior teaching day, not just paperwork.
Her **association action** and conditional library application reflect both solidarity and household arithmetic.

steps.text: Bring tutor paid-hour figures to musicians association
Apply first disruption year if day goes and advertised library vacancy offers suitable pay and hours
Keep Saturday choir job while seeking replacement work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the centre director to show every tutor which paid hours the new booking and practice tools replace. I would bring the timetables to the musicians association rather than argue with one parent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre pays me for registering pupils, preparing simple parts and checking practice recordings. If those jobs go, one of my two paid days may go with them, and four months of savings would not cover a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the other tutors to compare our paid hours and take the figures to the association meeting. In the first year of the change, if the centre cuts a day, I'll apply for a library music-room attendant vacancy if one opens while keeping Saturday choir work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because losing a whole day would make the mortgage tight. I have some savings and a few local posts to try, so I am not helpless. A computer can mark practice notes, but the mortgage still wants a person to pay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the library position actually open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library posted an attendant job last year, but I do not know whether it will open again. I'd ask for the actual rate and hours before assuming it helps the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you require before using pupils' recordings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put a child's practice recording into a tool I have never checked. If the centre wants that, it must get family permission and tell tutors where the files go.

say: I'd demand a written **2028 staffing plan** before centre hours change.
I'd keep **paid choir work** while human performers are still booked.
think: **AGI in 2028** could take centre thinking work before robots play around 2031.
Sam's **depot wage** will not cover our mortgage if my teaching day goes.
do: Get the **centre contract** and ask when next year's hours are set now.
Ask the **credit union** for written total hardship cost before accepting terms in the first year after 2028 if a day goes.
Apply for an **open library post** in the first year after 2028 only if net pay replaces the lost centre day.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible teaching-day loss, with four months of savings to search.
S2.quote: Four months of savings is a cushion, not four years of mortgage payments.
fieldNote: She sees **2028 thinking-work risk** before robot performers arrive around 2031.
Her **credit union and library** options both require full-cost checks before she commits to a new payment or job.

steps.text: Ask centre when next year's paid hours are set
Ask credit union first year after 2028 for written total cost if teaching day goes
Apply in first year after 2028 for open library post if net pay replaces lost day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to put the 2028 staffing plan on paper before selling parents a new teaching system. I would keep accompanying the choir while a human choir still has a paid place for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 could plan lessons, mark recordings and answer families better and cheaper than I do. Robots that can play hands-on parts arrive around 2031, but my centre hours could disappear first; Sam's depot pay cannot carry the mortgage and two children alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get my centre contract and ask the director when next year's hours are set. In the first year after 2028, if I lose a teaching day, I'll ask the credit union about temporary mortgage terms and apply for an open library job, keeping the choir unless its contract ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possibility of losing a teaching day, but I can ask about nearby posts. Four months of savings is a cushion, not four years of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the credit union before accepting help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit union has a hardship desk, but I would ask about total interest before accepting a new payment plan. I do not want a cheaper month to turn into years of extra debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any library vacancy actually replace the lost pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A library vacancy is possible, not promised. I would ask for the rate and hours, and take it only if it pays more after travel than the lost teaching day.

say: I'd ask for **funded repair training** while centre hours still pay the mortgage.
I'd tell colleagues **repair work** buys time, not permanent safety from robots.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens centre plans before hands-on robots arrive around 2034.
A **repair course** helps only if grant, childcare and real shop placements align.

Enrol before 2031 only if **grant funding**, shop acceptance and a class time compatible with Sam's childcare are confirmed.
Apply for a **paid shop placement** in the first year after 2031 only if qualified and a vacancy opens.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a course cannot promise a shop wage.
S3.quote: I will not buy a toolkit for a placement that has not opened.
fieldNote: Her **five-year window** makes a limited repair course possible without assuming robots stop in 2034.
She requires **grant funding**, childcare cover, accepted qualification and a real vacancy before spending.

steps.text: Ask college about grant and shop-accepted repair certificate
Enrol before 2031 if grant covers fees, shops accept certificate and class fits childcare
Apply for paid shop placement first year after 2031 if qualified and vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the centre and association for paid training over the five-year warning. I would rather learn to repair the keyboards children break than pretend I enjoy teaching through a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could do the lesson plans and practice checks, while robots able to do hands-on repair come around 2034. Repair is not a permanent refuge, but a few years might let me earn while I find more stable school work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the adult college whether a keyboard repair course has a grant and whether local shops accept its certificate. Before 2031 I'll enrol only if the grant covers fees and Sam can cover childcare; in the first year after AGI, I'll apply for a paid shop placement if I qualify and one opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the extra time gives me a route, not a guarantee. I still need the teaching days to pay the mortgage while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the class fit childcare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam works early at the depot on two weekdays, so I would need an evening class on another day. If that is not offered, I will wait for the next course rather than pay a sitter we cannot afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a placement or equipment be available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop owner I know said the placement list fills quickly. I would ask about vacancies before buying tools, and I would borrow college equipment during training. I will not buy a toolkit for a placement that has not opened.

say: I'd seek **paid school work** that values face-to-face music support.
I'd ask the centre to keep a **junior tutor place** while training routes grow.

Robot players around **2039** may reach hands-on work, so I need paid school hours.

fieldNote: Her **four-month reserve** supports gradual training without treating volunteer work as wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the choir a decade gives me time to build steadier work and still play beside them. I would also ask the centre to keep a paid junior tutor place for people who learn by doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, I will still owe on the mortgage and cannot treat retirement as a plan. Robots around 2039 could play or repair, so I need school support hours that do not depend on demo editing or practice sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask two nearby schools what credentials they require for a paid classroom music aide post. If a grant pays for the accepted course and the schedule fits childcare, I'll take it before 2036; I'll switch only for written paid hours that cover mortgage and travel. In the first year after AGI, I'll keep centre lessons only if families still book and school hours allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about what paid music becomes, but the longer notice lets me train without draining the reserve. Sam's wage and four months saved give us time to check an offer properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a school role worth leaving the centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not leave the centre for a volunteer position at a school. The school must offer paid hours in writing, and I would compare the net pay with travel and mortgage costs before switching. A volunteer badge from a school will not pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would older children change your plan now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our younger child will be older then, but I cannot budget around a future childcare saving now. I will keep the four-month reserve for real bills until school income is signed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the centre could cut a teaching day before I find paid work elsewhere. A written staffing plan, honest credit union terms and an actual library vacancy would let us decide before missing a mortgage bill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a free course includes childcare. A grant for fees is useful, but my partner and I still need someone to watch our children while I train.

headlineQuote: A grant for fees is useful, but my partner and I still need someone to watch our children while I train.
portrait: Zoe is a **43-year-old** junior musician with secondary education, teaching recorder, copying parts and accompanying a choir.
She and Sam have **two children**, a mortgage and about four months saved, with some nearby music posts.
She avoids **AI tools** and expects centre thinking tasks to shrink before robots reach hands-on music three years later.
She seeks **written hours**, collective records and funded training only when childcare and paid vacancies are real.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because a cut centre day could precede any replacement work.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing plan**, clear credit union costs and an open library post would help protect mortgage payments.
